explanations.aberdeen-act-1845--eusebio-de-queiros-la: The sources put the two together and put the resentment on the record: the government was against the British pressure — the seizure of Brazilian ships by British warships — and legislated under it anyway, five years after the Act and this time with enforcement behind the text. The law of 1831 had been a dead letter for nineteen years; what changed between 1831 and 1850 was not Brazilian opinion about slavery, which did not change until much later, but the cost of continuing.
explanations.berlin-conference--first-italo-ethiopian: The same section, listing the African states still independent after the conference, says Ethiopia fended off an Italian invasion from Eritrea in the First Italo-Ethiopian War of 1895–1896 and fell to Italian occupation in 1936 after defeat in the second. Eritrea is a colony of the scramble the General Act regulated, and the article names both wars as what became of Ethiopia in it.
explanations.berlin-conference--heligoland-zanzibar-t: The English article says the treaty served Chancellor Leo von Caprivi's aims for a settlement with the British, and that after the 1884 Berlin Conference Germany had been losing out in the scramble for Africa: the German East Africa Company had a strip of the Tanganyikan coast but no control over the Zanzibar sultanate's islands. The position the conference left Germany in is what the article gives as the reason the bargain was worth making.
explanations.berlin-conference--second-boer-war--prec: The English article on the conference lists, under its own aftermath, the states that were independent as of 1895 and were annexed by the British Empire roughly a decade after it — the two Boer republics among them — and says the Boer republics were conquered by the British in the Second Boer War of 1899 to 1902. The General Act the conference signed is what the article says regulated European colonisation and trade in Africa and agreed a common framework for recognising effective occupation; it does not say the conference decided this war, and this is drawn as a precondition for that reason.
explanations.boxer-rebellion--xinhai-revolution--prec: The claim is narrow: the Boxer settlement did not make the revolution of 1911, but it made the ground it happened on. The court came out of 1901 owing an indemnity it could only pay by taxing the provinces harder, garrisoned by foreign troops, and visibly unable to protect the country it claimed the mandate to rule. The reforms it then attempted — new armies, provincial assemblies, the end of the examinations — created both the officers who mutinied at Wuchang and the assemblies that declared for the republic. No source here argues a direct link, and none is asserted.
explanations.cuban-war-of-independence-1895-1898--spa: The two are the same conflict for its last three months, which is how the cited accounts put it: major escalation as American forces were deployed to Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines. The mechanism between them is documented and is not only the Maine. Weyler’s reconcentration camps killed a tenth of the population; the Cuban Junta in Florida ran a propaganda campaign in the American press and funded and smuggled arms; and the American papers, W. Joseph Campbell argues, exaggerated the atrocities to sell copies, though Andrea Pitzer notes the turn to savagery was real.
explanations.donghak-peasant-revolution--first-sino-j: The English article says the alarmed Joseon government asked the Qing dynasty for military intervention against the rebellion, that the Qing deployed 2,700 soldiers, and that Japan — angered that the Qing had not notified it beforehand as the Convention of Tientsin promised — started the First Sino-Japanese War. The account of the siege of Jeonju repeats it: on 3 May 1,500 Qing troops and 6,000 Japanese troops landed at Incheon the same day, and the Japanese question about the Convention of Tientsin "soon caused the First Sino-Japanese War".
explanations.empire-of-brazil-1822-1889--proclamation: The English article on the proclamation says the coup of 15 November 1889 abolished the constitutional monarchy of the Empire of Brazil and ended the reign of Emperor Pedro II, establishing the First Brazilian Republic in its place.
explanations.eusebio-de-queiros-law-1850--lei-aurea-1: Closing the traffic did not free anybody — the sources are emphatic that slavery stood for another thirty-eight years and that Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end it. What closing the traffic did was fix the size of the enslaved population and start it falling, against manumission, against the free-birth law of 1871, against the sexagenarian law of 1885, and against European immigrant labour arriving from the 1880s. Thirty-eight years is the interval between an institution losing its supply and losing its defenders.
explanations.first-italo-ethiopian-war--second-italo-: The English article on the war of 1935 begins its background with the war of 1896: Italy began its attempts to establish colonies in the Horn of Africa in the 1880s, and the first phase of that expansion concluded with the disastrous First Italo-Ethiopian War and the defeat at Adwa on 1 March 1896, after which Italy abandoned its expansionist plans in the area and limited itself to Eritrea and Somaliland for the next few decades.
explanations.first-sino-japanese-war--boxer-rebellion: The English article on the Boxer rebellion opens its account of the causes with that war: following the First Sino-Japanese war, villagers in North China feared the expansion of foreign spheres of influence and resented Christian missionaries who ignored local customs and used their power to protect their followers in court. The fear of the concessions that followed the defeat is the ground the article says the movement spread over from 1899.
explanations.first-sino-japanese-war--russo-japanese-: The English article on the Russo-Japanese war puts the First Sino-Japanese war at the head of its own account: at the end of that war the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895 had ceded the Liaodong Peninsula and Port Arthur to Japan before the Triple Intervention, in which Russia, Germany and France forced Japan to relinquish the claim. Japan then feared that Russia would impede its plans to establish a sphere of influence in mainland Asia, especially as Russia built the Trans-Siberian Railroad, made inroads in Korea, and acquired a lease of the Liaodong Peninsula and Port Arthur from China in 1898 — the rivalry over Manchuria and Korea the article says the war of 1904 was fought over.
explanations.franco-russian-alliance--world-war-i--pr: The English article says Russia and France entered the war united by the treaty of alliance, and that this had a significant effect on the course and outcome of the war since it forced Germany from the first days to fight on two fronts, leading to the defeat at the First Battle of the Marne and the collapse of the Schlieffen Plan. The article puts the alliance among the causes of the shape the war took, not among the causes of its outbreak.
explanations.greco-turkish-war-of-1897--first-balkan-: The English article draws the line itself: the public awareness in Greece of the country’s unpreparedness for a war in pursuit of its national aspirations "laid the seeds for the Goudi coup of 1909, which called for immediate reforms in the Greek Army, economy, and society", and when Eleftherios Venizelos came to power he instigated the reforms that transformed the Greek state, "leading it to victory in the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 three years later". The claim is narrow and it is the article’s: the defeat of 1897 is a precondition of the army Greece fought with in 1912, not a cause of the war.
explanations.heligoland-zanzibar-treaty--anglo-zanzib: The English article says that in return for what it gave up Germany recognised British authority in Zanzibar, that Britain "immediately declared a protectorate over Zanzibar", and that "in the subsequent 1896 Anglo-Zanzibar War, gained full control of the sultanate". The treaty is what put Britain in the position the war was fought from; the article does not argue that it caused the war.
explanations.heligoland-zanzibar-treaty--entente-cord: The English article runs one line from the treaty to 1904: the treaty acquired Heligoland, an island strategically placed for control over the German Bight; with the Kiel Canal building from 1887, control of the Bight "had become essential to Emperor Wilhelm's II plans for expansion of the Imperial Navy"; and "Wilhelm's naval policies aborted an accommodation with the British and ultimately led to a rapprochement between Britain and France, sealed with the Entente cordiale in 1904". The naval policy and not the treaty is what the article says drove Britain to France, so this is a precondition and nothing stronger.
explanations.independence-of-brazil-1822--aberdeen-ac: Independence turned an obligation between Britain and Portugal into one between Britain and Brazil, and it did so on British terms: recognition was the thing Brazil needed and the convention of 1826 on the abolition of the trade is what it cost. The Act of 1845 is legislation against a state that exists, over a convention that state signed, and neither the state nor the convention exists without 1822.
explanations.independence-of-brazil-1822--empire-of-b: The English article on the Empire begins with the declaration: on 7 September 1822 Pedro declared the independence of Brazil and, after waging a successful war against his father’s kingdom, was acclaimed on 12 October as Pedro I, the first Emperor of Brazil.
explanations.jameson-raid--second-boer-war--precondit: The article says it in the lead, in those words: **"the raid was a contributory cause of the Second Boer War."** What it contributed is listed just before — the raid of 29 December 1895 "was intended to trigger an uprising by the primarily British expatriate and settler workers (known as Uitlanders) in the Transvaal, but it failed", and its results "included embarrassment of the British government; the replacement of Cecil Rhodes as prime minister of the Cape Colony; and **the strengthening of Boer dominance of the Transvaal and its gold mines**". The edge is `precondition-of` because "contributory cause" is what the article claims and no more.
explanations.lei-aurea-1888--proclamation-of-the-braz: Eighteen months, and the sources name the mechanism rather than leaving it to be inferred: the Empire lost the political support of the large landowners because of the abolition of 1888, which was carried without compensating the slaveholders, and the slaveholding agrarian elite took it as a personal act of the imperial family. The monarchy was deposed by army officers, not by planters; but it was deposed without anyone defending it, and this is why nobody did.
explanations.philippine-revolution--philippine-americ: The English article on the war says it emerged in early 1899 following the American annexation of the islands, and that Philippine nationalists "had proclaimed independence in June 1898 and constituted the First Philippine Republic in January 1899" — neither of which the United States recognised as legitimate, tensions escalating until fighting began at Manila on 4 February. The republic the Americans refused to recognise is what the revolution of 1896 had made; that is the precondition claimed here, and nothing more.
explanations.philippine-revolution--philippine-declar: The article's § History begins the story at the revolution: "in 1896, the Philippine Revolution began. In December 1897, the Spanish government and the revolutionaries signed a truce, the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, requiring that the Spaniards pay the revolutionaries $MXN800,000 and that Aguinaldo and other leaders go into exile in Hong Kong." The declaration of 12 June 1898 "was proclaimed by Filipino revolutionary forces general Emilio Aguinaldo… It asserted the sovereignty and independence of the Philippine islands from the 300 years of colonial rule by Spain": the same movement, the same general, back from the exile the truce sent him into.
explanations.proclamation-of-the-brazilian-republic-1:
Seventy-five years, and the claim is about a pattern rather than about a plan. The Republic was founded on 15 November 1889 by army officers deposing a head of state without firing a shot, and the political life of the First Republic it began ran from 1889 to 1930. Wikipedia’s account of 1964 reports Alfred Stepan’s model of the Brazilian army as a moderating power — a force that overthrows civil governments and installs new ones — and says that what was new in 1964 was the officers keeping the power instead of handing it on, breaking the pattern rather than beginning it. The edge says that 1889 is where that pattern starts and that 1964 is the last act of the period it defines. It does not say the one produced the other.

Why this is `probable` and not `consensus`, although it cites a named scholar: the atlas has one source here, not two. Stepan is where the claim comes from and Wikipedia is where this run read him. An encyclopedia reporting an author is not a second author agreeing with him, which is what amendment A2 is about and what rule 9 asks for.

What 1930 ended was what 1889 began: an oligarchic republic in which the presidency passed between São Paulo and Minas Gerais by arrangement, and which the sources call a four-decade hegemony. Two things carried over from the proclamation and are the shape of 1930 as well — that the army makes and unmakes governments in Brazil, the Republic itself having been a bloodless military coup, and that the electorate was a census electorate. Vargas came in as the candidate who had lost the election.
explanations.second-boer-war--entente-cordiale--preco: The English article's background says the situation for Britain and France changed in the last decade of the nineteenth century, and that "the change had its roots in a British loss of confidence after the Second Boer War and a growing fear of the strength of Germany". The article also names what had kept the two apart — the scramble for Africa and the Fashoda incident of 1898, over which France backed down — and records that Britain decided not to join the Triple Alliance and revived the idea of a French alliance instead.
explanations.second-boer-war--treaty-of-windsor--caus: The secret declaration signed at Windsor on 14 October 1899 is dated three days after the war began, and its two undertakings are the war's: Portugal would close Lourenço Marques and the railway to arms and men bound for the Transvaal, and Britain would guarantee Portugal's colonies. Britain needed the port shut because it was the only one the Boer republics could reach without crossing British ground; Portugal needed the guarantee because Britain and Germany had secretly agreed the year before how to divide the Portuguese colonies if Lisbon defaulted on its debts. Ramos and Meneses both read the declaration as bought by the war rather than as an act of sentiment about the alliance of 1386, which is the claim here.
explanations.slave-trade-act-1807--aberdeen-act-1845-: Having closed its own trade, Britain set about closing everyone else’s: the cited account of the Act says it encouraged British action to press other states to abolish their own. The Aberdeen Act is thirty-eight years of that policy arriving at the largest remaining market, with the Royal Navy authorised to take Brazilian ships as pirates. `precondition-of` rather than `caused`: 1807 did not require 1845, and what made 1845 happen was a lapsed convention and a tariff quarrel. But a power that still ran its own slave trade could not have legislated for anybody else’s.
explanations.slave-trade-act-1807--slavery-abolition-: The Act of 1807 outlawed the trade and not the institution, and many of its supporters expected the one to finish the other; it did not. What followed instead was a twenty-six-year apparatus — the Slave Trade Felony Act of 1811 making the overseas traffic a felony, the West Africa Squadron sent to suppress it, the Anti-Slavery Society founded in 1823, the Colonial Office rejecting colonial slave legislation as it arrived in London. 1833 is where that apparatus finally reached the thing itself. `precondition-of`: the first act made the second thinkable and did not make it happen.
explanations.spanish-american-war-1898--philippine-de: What brought Aguinaldo back from Hong Kong was the American war, and the article says how: **"in April 1898, shortly after the beginning of the Spanish–American War, Commodore George Dewey, aboard the USS *Olympia*, sailed into Manila Bay, leading the Asiatic Squadron of the US Navy. On May 1, 1898, the US defeated the Spaniards in the Battle of Manila Bay. Emilio Aguinaldo decided to return to the Philippines to help American forces defeat the Spaniards. The US Navy agreed to transport him back aboard the USS *McCulloch*."** Six weeks later he declared independence. The article is equally plain that the war did not ratify it — "the declaration was never recognized by either the US or Spain. Instead, Spain ceded the Philippines to the United States in the 1898 Treaty of Paris" — which is why the edge is `enabled` and not `caused`.
explanations.spanish-american-war-1898--platt-amendme: The Amendment exists to answer a question the war created: on what terms do the American troops in Cuba leave. It sets seven conditions for their withdrawal and an eighth requiring Cuba to sign a treaty accepting the other seven, and the Treaty of Paris had already set Cuba up as an independent state in 1902 that was a protectorate in practice. The occupation had been the McKinley administration’s answer, in 1899, to the appearance of a revolutionary government on the island; the Amendment is how it ended without ending.
explanations.spanish-american-war-1898--treaty-of-par: The English article opens by saying the treaty was signed by Spain and the United States on 10 December 1898 and marked the official end of the Spanish–American War, and that under it Spain relinquished sovereignty over Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the cession of the Philippines involving a payment of twenty million dollars. A peace treaty caused by the war it ends is the plainest case the atlas holds of this edge type.
explanations.strangford-treaty-1810--aberdeen-act-184: The Aberdeen Act did not invent a British claim over the Brazilian traffic; it enforced one that had been conceded thirty-five years earlier. The 1810 treaty is where Portugal first agreed to limit the importation of Africans and to consider abolishing the trade, and the Anglo-Brazilian convention of 1826 — the instrument the 1845 Act names in its own long title as the thing it amends — is that concession inherited by the new empire. `precondition-of`: without the promise there is nothing for the Act to be the enforcement of.
explanations.the-amazon-rubber-boom--the-end-of-the-a: There is no monopoly to lose until something has made one. The boom is what built the extractive trade, the towns, the railway and the market position, and the position is exactly what plantation latex took away: a commodity gathered from wild trees scattered through forest could not be produced at the cost of one grown in rows. The two are one record split at the point the price fell.
explanations.the-amazon-rubber-boom--the-rubber-battl: The second boom went back to the forests the first had opened and found them nearly empty: after the first collapse no more than thirty-five thousand workers remained in the region, against the hundred thousand men the wartime quota needed. The tapping paths, the river towns and the trade’s whole apparatus were the first boom’s; what 1942 had to supply was the labour, and it took it from the Northeast by conscription.
explanations.the-amazon-rubber-boom--treaty-of-petrop: The English article says the treaty ended the Acre War between Bolivia and Brazil over the then-Bolivian territory of Acre, "a desirable territory in Bolivia-Brazil border during the contemporary rubber boom", and that Brazil took Acre in exchange for territory between the Abuna and the Madeira, two million pounds and a pledge to build a railway bypassing the rapids on the Madeira. What made the ground worth a war is what the article names, and it is the boom this atlas already holds. The article dates the signature 17 November 1903 and the record carries the item's own 11 November; neither was changed to match the other.
explanations.the-baptist-war-1831--slavery-abolition-: The causal statement is the cited account’s own: because of the loss of property and life in the rebellion of 1831, Parliament held two inquiries, and the results of those inquiries contributed greatly to the abolition of slavery in the Act of 1833. Twenty months from a strike put down in ten days to an act of Parliament. It is worth marking that the atlas can say this plainly while the same sources are still arguing about whether industrial capitalism or moral outrage ended the trade in 1807 — a specific, dated, documented mechanism is a different kind of claim from a thesis about an economy.
explanations.the-brazilian-coffee-cycle--companhia-si: The steelworks stands where the coffee was. Colonel Macedo Soares, who chaired the commission studying where to put a large mill, argued for the Paraíba valley, which had fallen into decadence with the decline of coffee in Rio de Janeiro state, and had the support of Amaral Peixoto, then interventor there. The claim is narrow and is meant to be: not that coffee produced steel, but that the ground the first industrial plant was set on had been cleared by the end of the crop that came before it.
explanations.the-brazilian-coffee-cycle--the-1930-rev: The politics 1930 overthrew is named after the crop. The second boom, from the 1880s to the 1930s, corresponds to the period called café com leite after the dominant industries of the two largest states, coffee in São Paulo and dairy in Minas Gerais, and coffee was three quarters of export earnings. Valorisation — the state buying the harvest to hold the price up, from Taubaté in 1906 — worked for the planters and the treasury, and produced a global oversupply that, on Wikipedia’s account, increased the damage the Depression did when it came. `precondition-of` rather than `caused`: the revolution had its own quarrel, and what the cycle supplied was the arrangement it was a quarrel with and the crash it happened in.
explanations.thousand-days-war--hay-bunau-varilla-tre: The article on the Colombian civil war says its repercussions included "the eventual loss of the Department of Panama as an incorporated territory of the republic in 1903", and that the American navy was sent by Roosevelt's government to protect United States interests in the construction of the Panama Canal. The treaty article says the United States intent to influence the area "led to the separation of Panama from Colombia in 1903 and its establishment as an independent state", and the treaty of 18 November 1903 was signed by the United States and that new state. A treaty between Washington and Panama was possible only because Panama had ceased to be Colombian, which is what the war ended in.
explanations.transfer-of-the-portuguese-court-to-braz: Wikipedia’s account is direct about it: the transfer "represented the first step toward Brazilian independence, since the prince regent immediately opened the ports of Brazil to foreign shipping and turned the colonial capital into the seat of government". Thirteen years of being the centre of an empire rather than a possession of one gave Brazil a treasury, a press, a bank, courts and an administration; when the Cortes in Lisbon set about undoing all of it after 1820, there was a state in Rio for Pedro to refuse on behalf of.

Britain escorted the Braganzas across the Atlantic and then presented the bill. The ports had been opened to friendly nations at Salvador in January 1808, which the sources read as one of the ways John found to repay British assistance; the treaty of 1810 turned that into a rate — fifteen per cent on British goods, below what Portugal itself paid — and into a standing obligation. A government in exile in its own colony, defended by somebody else’s navy, is the condition under which those terms were signable, and it is the transfer that produced it.
explanations.treaty-of-paris-1898--philippine-america: The English article on the war names the treaty as what it followed: the war "emerged in early 1899 following the United States’ annexation of the former Spanish colony of the Philippine Islands under the terms of the December 1898 Treaty of Paris". Spain sold to the United States an archipelago whose revolutionaries had declared independence six months earlier, and the war is what the transfer produced.
explanations.treaty-of-windsor--germany-declares-war-: Portugal went to war in 1916 because it seized German ships in the Tagus at British request, and it did that because the alliance obliged it and because the colonies it wanted kept were guaranteed by the same alliance. The declaration of 1899 is the last renewal of that guarantee before the war and the answer to the Anglo-German agreement of 1898 about how the Portuguese colonies might be divided. The edge is `precondition-of`: the alliance is what made a Portuguese belligerency thinkable and the colonies what made it desirable, and neither of those is the decision of February 1916.
